column4: The section's 94:1 chest is a widened vessel; this verse uses the same root in يشرح صدره for opening the chest to Islam, then contrasts it with a chest made tight and constricted.
The section begins with an expanded chest; this verse repeats شرح الصدر for a chest opened to Islam and sets it against hearts hardened at God's remembrance.
Moses asks رب اشرح لي صدري; the same chest-expansion image becomes a prayer for capacity before a demanding task.
The section's opened chest is a sign of increased capacity; here شرح بالكفر صدرا describes willingly opening the chest to disbelief, the reverse direction from the section's Godward image.
The section explicitly reads فؤاد أم موسى فارغا as an empty vessel, empty of patience after she puts her child in the water; the verse says God had to bind her heart to keep her steady.
The section explains pouring from a bucket as the source of the prayer أفرغ علينا صبرا; here Saul's followers use that exact plea for patience and firm feet before Goliath's forces.
The section quotes أفرغ علينا صبرا; here Pharaoh's threatened magicians pray those words for patience and ask to die as Muslims, making the pouring metaphor a plea under threat.
The section develops فرغ as pouring the contents of a vessel; after setting iron blocks between the two mountain sides, Dhul-Qarnayn says أفرغ عليه قطرا, pouring molten copper over the structure.
The section's empty heart is held together by God's support; here God says وربطنا على قلوبهم before the youths stand and declare that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and earth.

The section recalls Moses' mother placing her child in water; this verse makes the container explicit, ordering him placed in a box and cast into the river, which delivers him safely to shore rather than letting him be poured away.

The section uses 28:10's empty heart after Moses' mother parts from her child; this earlier verse supplies the act behind that state, telling her to nurse him and cast him into the river if she fears for him.
The section treats the chest as a vessel whose contents are brought out; this verse says what is in the chests is exposed, a direct inner-content parallel.
The section ends by turning desire toward the Lord and glosses راغب as desire; this verse says إنا إلى الله راغبون while speaking of God's and the Messenger's gifts from bounty.

The section joins desire toward the Lord to a great gift one longs for; after the garden owners lose their hoarded crop, they say إنا إلى ربنا راغبون and hope their Lord will replace it with something better.
The section's well, bucket, and gathered water meet a clear boundary here: if water sinks into the earth, who can bring accessible running water? The question turns dependence toward God.

The section's bucket and well scene has a concrete counterpart when a water-drawer lowers his bucket into a well; unexpectedly, it brings up Joseph rather than water, reversing the tool's ordinary purpose.
The section makes the heart a receptacle that can be empty of patience; here God sends tranquility into believers' hearts and increases their faith, an inward filling with steadiness.
The section brings water and a heart needing support together; here rain purifies the believers while God strengthens their hearts and steadies their feet.
The section reads فرغت as becoming free of an occupation and then turning toward God; this verse begins فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ الصَّلَاةُ, then sends people out to seek God's bounty.
The section's فراغ is the opposite of being occupied; this verse names the Prophet's سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا, a long daytime occupation, and 73:8 completes the movement by commanding devotion to his Lord.

The section moves from finishing to turning desire toward the Lord; this command to remember the Lord and وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا gives that Godward devotion, while 73:7 names the long daytime occupation.
The section's sequence frees a person from work and redirects attention to God; these people remain attentive to remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving even while trade and business could distract them.
The section says direct desire toward your Lord; this command tells the Prophet to stay with people who seek their Lord's face and not let his eyes turn toward worldly adornment.

The section glosses فراغ as the opposite of occupation; the different use سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ promises that God will attend to the two groups, reversing the direction of attention in the section's human turning toward God.
The section's رغبة is directed toward the Lord; the same root in يَرْغَبُ عَن مِلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ marks turning away from Abraham's way, the contrary direction.
The section directs desire toward the Lord; Ibrahim's father uses the same root in أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ آلِهَتِي to challenge Ibrahim for turning away from his gods, a specific opposite orientation.
The section's dictionary note calls a رغِيبة a great desired gift; here the Lord promises to give the Prophet until he is satisfied, a concrete instance of generous divine giving.
The section directs longing to the Lord and names a desired great gift; this command says the Lord's provision is better and more lasting than the worldly display one might covet.
The section records the secondary gloss of رغب as gluttony; this command permits eating and drinking but sets a boundary against excess, making appetite's limit explicit.
The section's secondary image is a wide-bellied, voracious eater; this verse depicts disbelievers eating as livestock eat and contrasts that immediate appetite with the Fire as their destination.

The section names gluttonous appetite and a much-desired gift; in the garden parable, the owners plan to exclude the poor from the crop, and 68:31-32 completes the scene with their remorse and renewed hope in their Lord.
The section connects appetite with a great desired gift; this verse says the human being is intense in love of wealth, and the same short passage proceeds to what is exposed in the chests at 100:10.
The section's vessel image brings hidden contents into view; this verse supplies the resurrection setting, when what lies in graves is scattered, before 100:10 names what is exposed in chests.
After the section's image of chest contents exposed at 100:10, this closing verse adds that their Lord is fully aware of them on that day, completing the disclosure with its divine witness.
The section's chest and bucket are images of a container emptied of what it holds; this verse says the earth casts out what is within it and empties itself, extending that action to the earth.
The section describes a vessel emptied of its contents; this repeated earth image says the earth brings out its burdens, a specific parallel of concealed contents being released.
The section moves water from a bucket toward a basin; here the floodwater subsides when earth is told to swallow its water and sky to stop, a large-scale reversal in which abundant water disappears.
The section's image is water collected in a broad basin; this verse says water is sent down in measure and settled in the earth, while God can also take it away.
The section develops a well and abundant gathered water; this verse traces water through the earth as springs, then shows the growth it sustains before the plants dry and break apart.
The section turns toward a plentiful water source; this garden owner fears its water may sink into the earth so deeply that it cannot be recovered, a specific boundary on abundance.
The section's stone basin and abundant water find a concrete water-source parallel when striking the rock makes twelve springs gush, with each group knowing its drinking place.
This repeated account of twelve springs gushing from a struck rock gives each tribe a known place to drink, matching the section's built water source and provision.
The section's wellhead image is echoed by the water point at Midian, where people water their flocks and two women hold theirs back; 28:24 completes the scene with Moses watering for them.
The section pictures turning toward abundant water; in the Midian well scene set at 28:23, Moses draws water for the two women, making the source a concrete provision for those waiting there.
The section turns its desire toward the Lord; Noah tells his people to seek forgiveness from their Lord, and 71:11-12 completes the appeal with promised rain, gardens, rivers, wealth, and children.
The section's gathered water and desired abundance meet the promise يرسل السماء عليكم مدرارا, abundant rain after the appeal to seek the Lord in 71:10; 71:12 adds gardens and rivers.
The section links the Lordward desire to a great gift and abundant water; this verse promises wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, completing the rain promise in 71:11.
The section's spacious basin holds abundant water toward which one turns; this verse promises that a people who remain on the right path will be given مَاءً غَدَقًا, abundant water.
The section's abundant water is a desired provision; the next verse says it is also a test and warns whoever turns from remembrance of his Lord, giving a boundary to the promise in 72:16.
The section moves between bucket, basin, and water source; this verse describes a spring from which God's servants drink and which they make gush abundantly.
The section's water vessel and source meet in this cup scene: cups, ewers, and a drink from a flowing spring are served to the people of the Garden.
The section's bucket and basin sequence includes pouring liquid; this verse says a spring of molten copper was made to flow for Solomon, and 34:13 continues with enormous basins and fixed pots.

The section names a spacious basin as part of its water image; this verse depicts جِفَانٍ كَالْجَوَابِ, huge basins like reservoirs, alongside fixed cooking pots. The preceding 34:12 supplies the flowing copper source.
The section shows molten copper poured over an iron structure to strengthen it; here molten copper is sent upon the two as a punishment, reversing the material's role.
The section develops water being poured from a vessel and abundant water as provision; this verse describes copious rain pouring down, and 78:15 gives the resulting grain and plants.
The section glosses emptying a bucket as pouring out what it contains; this verse depicts water poured down in abundance, with 80:26-32 continuing through crops and food as its provision.
The section turns toward a plentiful water source; this verse asks about the water people drink, while 56:69 names its descent and 56:70 the possibility of its becoming undrinkable.
The section joins a water source to desire for the Lord; this verse asks whether people send down their drinking water or God does, and 56:70 supplies the boundary that God could make it bitter.
The section's wide basin and desired water signify abundance; this verse says God could make drinking water bitter, completing the preceding question about who sends it down.
The section figures the expanded chest as increased capacity; this verse says God charges no soul beyond its capacity, giving a specific limit to that image.
The section presents Musa's mother's heart as empty of patience and then bound; this verse says hearts find reassurance in remembering God, a specific account of how an inward state becomes settled.
After asking for his chest to be opened in 20:25, Moses asks that his task be made easy; this next step makes the expanded chest's practical purpose explicit.
The section's closing movement is to turn toward one's Lord after exertion; this command to the Prophet says to be patient for his Lord, joining effort, patience, and Lordward orientation.
The section glosses رغِيبة as a great gift one would desire; this verse calls the reward from the Lord a measured and ample gift, a specific divine-gift counterpart.
